No. US military members are compensated pretty well already, at least now. While some complain about the base pay - and it's not great, to be sure - those same people neglect to mention:

-Housing and utilities* are covered, tax-free (either with gov't-provided housing or via housing allowances). At least stateside, an eligible service member who is smart can live in civilian housing for less than the allowance and pocket the difference.

*there were rumblings a few years ago about making service members pay for utilities in gov't housing; I don't know what came of that, if anything.

Food is provided for, again tax-free, either via mess halls or an allowance. The food allowance isn't much, but again, a smart service member can cover most, if not all, of their monthly food budget with that allowance.

-Medical is provided for, also tax-free and at little-to-no out-of-pocket expense to the service member, and also covers families. Reserve/Guard medical coverage works a bit differently, but it's a grest deal for active duty. As with anything, the effectiveness varies with location and who your doctor is, but my experiences with Navy medical were pretty positive.

-Enlisted members receive an annual uniform allowance, again tax-free. A smart service member will take proper care of his uniforms and not need to spend a bunch of money to maintain his uniforms.

-Active duty members get 30 days of leave (that is, paid vacation) per year, accrued at 2.5 days per month (whether or not you get to use it is another story...). Convalescent leave (that is, time off to recover from serious injury, illness, or surgery) is not deducted from your regular leave.

-Tuition assistance is available (again, whether or not you get to use it is a different story...). It is entirely possible to complete a two-year degree while on active duty; I've heard of (but not seen) people finishing Bachelor's degrees in a single four-year enlistment. Also, many colleges will give you credits for some of the official training courses you'll go through, and some of the correspondence courses provided by the military are ACE-accredited, which can net more college credits depending on the school.

-Speaking of military training, depending on your job, it can be world-class or hot garbage. There are also apprenticeship paths available via the military wherein you can receive journeyman status or qualify for certain industry-recognized professional certifications.
